newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany must wait for real jobs upswing-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Germany must wait for real jobs upswing-analysts.

text.p: The long-awaited upswing in Germany's lethargic economy could start finally to translate into shorter dole queues when labour market figures for May are released on Friday.
But most analysts say the upswing is so sluggish that they are loth to talk of a real turnaround in the trend behind the worst jobs crisis the Federal Republic has known.
A genuine turnaround will not come until later in the year, they told Reuters on Tuesday.

Christine Walter at Commerzbank in Frankfurt said: "The improvement in the economy will only make itself felt on the jobs market very slowly -- by late summer with job seekers and by the end of the year for the unemployed. It will be late summer before we see a turnaround in the trend."
She forecast a rise of 5,000 in the seasonally-adjusted jobless number.
Pan-German seasonally-adjusted unemployment rose by 8,000 to 4.299 million in April and German jobless figures have been at or near post-war record levels since the start of the year.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Monday that the economic upswing should cause a turnaround in the jobs market by the end of 1997. He said the continued high level of unemployment was the biggest single challenge facing his government.
Holger Fahrinkrug, analyst at UBS, does not expect a dramatic change by the end of the year.

"We only really expect a small change by the end of the year -- that means no serious increase in the numbers of unemployed. We do have the worst behind us," said Fahrinkrug, who forecast a drop of 15,000 in May.
Some analysts are more upbeat about labour market prospects this year.

Armin Kayser at SBC Warburg said: "We are near a turnaround in the jobs market. Growth in industry has become more dynamic, and there is now a real chance that that the German government's jobless forecast for the year will be undershot."
His outlook is for a drop of 15,000 in the seasonally-adjusted figure in May.
Economist Harald Joerg of Dresdner Bank said in a study that because of the broadening of production in the economy and less pressure from rationalisation, a moderate fall in unemployment was likely.
"The numbers of unemployed will average 4.25 million in the current year and will fall to around 4.1 million in 1998; the rate will stay above 10 percent in 1998 as well," Joerg said.
"The high levels of unemployment which have built up over the last 20 years will not disappear in just a couple of years."

In western Germany in April, the number of people out of work on a seasonally adjusted basis rose by 6,000 to 3.016 million. Eastern Germany added 2,000 to unemployment rolls, reaching a total 1.284 million.
Stefan Bergheim of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson does not expect a change in the jobless figures in May, despite the normal seasonal boost for the labour market.
"We were very disappointed with the April figures for the jobs market. The best we can really hope for is for the situation to stabilise, but we cannot expect an improvement."
Lothar Hessler at Trinkaus Capital Management also remains pessimistic. "The jobs market is suffering the effects of structural problems."

"The situation which began at the start of the year is not just a temporary one. The most important factor would be increased flexibility in the jobs market. Economic growth is just passing the jobs market by," said Hessler, who anticipates a fall of 2,000 in the jobless figures in May.
